title: Towards Understanding Adam Convergence on Highly Degenerate Polynomials
claim: Optimizer convergence behavior differs by objective: on strongly convex losses the adaptive method is unstable, while on degenerate losses it converges fastest.
layout: 2 side-by-side log-scale loss plots, left-to-right, function formula captions beneath
description: Two side-by-side line plots show loss on a log scale against epoch (0 to 10000) for four optimizers: GD (solid blue), GD Momentum (dashed orange), SignGD (green) and Adam (red). A dotted black line marks the reference level L(η/2). Panel (a) is captioned L(x)=½x² (strongly convex). Adam, in red, drops fastest, then spikes at around epoch 2300 and oscillates near the SignGD plateau. GD and Momentum decline steadily and linearly in log scale. Panel (b) is captioned L(x)=¼x⁴ (degenerate). GD and Momentum barely move, SignGD plateaus quickly, and Adam falls in a straight line on the log scale to about 1e-45, far below the others. The red Adam curve draws the eye first, and the legends sit inside each plot.
caption: Convergence behavior differs between strongly convex and degenerate polynomials. Adam uses $\beta_1=0.9, \beta_2=0.99$.
abstract: Adam is a widely used optimization algorithm in deep learning, yet the specific class of objective functions where it exhibits inherent advantages remains underexplored. Unlike prior studies requiring external schedulers and $Î²_2$ near 1 for convergence, this work investigates the ``natural'' auto-convergence properties of Adam. We identify a class of highly degenerate polynomials where Adam converges automatically without additional schedulers. Specifically, we derive theoretical conditions for local asymptotic stability on degenerate polynomials and demonstrate strong alignment between theoretical bounds and experimental results. We prove that Adam achieves local linear convergence on these degenerate functions, significantly outperforming the sub-linear convergence of Gradient Descent and Momentum. This acceleration stems from a decoupling mechanism between the second moment $v_t$ and squared gradient $g_t^2$, which exponentially amplifies the effective learning rate. Finally, we characterize Adam's hyperparameter phase diagram, identifying three distinct behavioral regimes: stable convergence, spikes, and SignGD-like oscillation.
